successors.name: Kingdom of Alba
successors.text: Ayrshire and part of Galloway, the last shape (5,341 km2): Cliopatria's Kingdom of Alba row holds all 19 cells in 1236

ledger.x: 439: Cliopatria's Britons hold the island south of the Forth-Clyde and north-west Armorica.
441: the Chronica Gallica of 452 records Saxon rule over the eastern provinces.

c. 450: Deira is established on land the Britons held. Infobox 'Established: c. 450'; 'The kingdom, which was previously ruled by a British dynasty, was probably created in the third quarter of the fifth century when Anglian warriors invaded the Derwent Valley'. The kingdom-of-deira dossier founds the kingdom c. 450…

c. 455: Kent is established. Infobox 'Established: c. 455'; 'According to the Chronicle, in 455 Hengist and Horsa fought Vortigern at Ægelesthrep (probably Aylesford in Kent)'; 'they established their Kingdom in East Kent'; before it 'the area of modern Kent that lay east of the River Medway was a civitas known as…
477: Ælle founds the South Saxons' kingdom on land the Britons held.
480: the Saxons widen their hold south of the Thames and in the north.

c. 540: Gwynedd is on the map. Gwynedd has 'a semi-legendary origin in the arrival of Cunedda from Manau Gododdin in the fifth century' and Maelgwn Gwynedd was 'condemned by Gildas c. 540'. Cliopatria cuts 24 cells for it from the Brythons shape.
540: Cliopatria's Powys row begins.
540: Cliopatria's Brycheiniog row begins.
540: Cliopatria's Gwent row begins.
540: Cliopatria's Morgannwg (Glywysing) row begins; the page gives no formation date (page silent).
547: Ida takes the throne of Bernicia at Bamburgh.

c. 550: Rheged is on the map. 'Urien Rheged, (c. 550 - 590), about whom survive eight songs of Taliesin'; 'a late 6th-century king of Rheged'; 'a kingdom covering a large part of modern Cumbria'. No page gives a founding year, so 550 is the start of Urien's dated reign and the extent before 592 is unknown (confidence…
577: Ceawlin takes Gloucester, Cirencester and Bath at Dyrham.
577: the Hwicce kingdom is established on 13 of the cells that leave.
587: Brittany leaves the Brythons shape.
592: Cliopatria's Dunoting row begins on 6 cells of the Brythons shape (none of them in the 592 shape).
602: Dumnonia is drawn as its own kingdom.
617: Cliopatria gives Mercia 14 cells of the Britons' Cheshire and north Staffordshire.

628: Cliopatria's Mercia shape takes 22 more cells of the Britons' Shropshire, Black Country, Staffordshire and Herefordshire border; the Brythons shape lets them go in 633, the year of 'the disastrous Battle of Hatfield Chase on 12 October 633' on the Bernicia page.
638: Edinburgh falls to the Angles.
638: Cliopatria's Rheged shape grows by 2 cells that were in the Brythons shape (the brythons_638 shape loses 27 cells: 25 to Northumbria, 2 to Rheged).
644: Strathclyde is drawn as its own kingdom.
875: 17 cells of the Britons' south-west Wales (the shape falls from 25,043 to 20,444 km2 as drawn) lie in Cliopatria's Kingdom of Gwynedd 875 shape.

c. 900: Strathclyde takes the land west of the Pennines. 'Around the year 900, after the power of Northumbria was destroyed by Viking incursions and settlement' large areas west of the Pennines came under Strathclyde. Cliopatria draws the gain in 870 (see brythons_870).
911: Cliopatria's Seisyllwg shape grows over 10 of the Britons' south-west Welsh cells.
936: Cliopatria gives the English the Britons' land south of the Eamont.
960: the Seisyllwg land becomes Brythons' again in Cliopatria.
1056: Cliopatria's Gwynedd shape reaches over 27 cells of the Britons' south-west Wales until 1065.
1066: the 27 cells return to the Britons in Cliopatria when Gwynedd's shape shrinks.
1085: Cliopatria gives Norman England 17 cells of the Britons' south-west Wales.
1092: William II takes Carlisle and Cumberland.
1094: the Normans hold most of Wales.
1216: Cliopatria's Gwynedd shape takes 9 cells of the Britons' south-west Wales, which the Brythons shape gives up in 1227.
1235: the last Brythons shape, Ayrshire and Galloway, is no longer drawn; Cliopatria's Kingdom of Alba row takes all 19 cells in 1236.

wars.name: Anglo-Saxon settlement of Britain
wars.outcome: The Britons lose the Saxon-held east in 441 and a further 145 cells by 480; until the 570s they 'were still in control of about half of England and Wales' (Sub-Roman Britain); the period ends with Deorham in 577.

wars.name: Battle of Deorham
wars.outcome: West Saxon victory: three British kings killed and three cities taken, the single Chronicle entry '577'.

wars.name: Battle of Chester
wars.outcome: Æthelfrith of Northumbria 'annihilated a combined force from the Welsh kingdoms of Powys and Rhôs'; Selyf ap Cynan of Powys killed; about 1,200 monks of Bangor-on-Dee killed (Bede).

wars.name: Northumbrian conquest of Elmet
wars.outcome: Edwin 'led an invasion of Elmet, and overran it in 616 or 617'; 'the realm was incorporated into Northumbria on Easter in 627'.

wars.name: Cadwallon's invasion of Northumbria
wars.outcome: Hatfield Chase on 12 October 633 was 'disastrous' for Northumbria, which was 'divided back into Bernicia and Deira'; Oswald 'defeated Cadwallon at the Battle of Heavenfield in 634' and reunited Northumbria.

wars.name: Siege of Edinburgh
wars.outcome: 'In 638, Eidyn, modern Edinburgh, was under siege and fell to the Angles'; the Gododdin come under Bernicia's rule 'around this time'.

wars.name: Battle of Strathcarron
wars.outcome: 'the Britons of Alt Clut led by Eugein son of Beli defeated the men of Dál Riata' and killed Domnall Brecc; no land change recorded.

wars.name: Siege of Dumbarton
wars.outcome: The Norse besieged Alt Clut; the siege 'led to the destruction of the citadel and the taking of a very large number of captives'; the capital moved to Govan.

wars.name: Battle of Brunanburh
wars.outcome: 'In 937 he joined Constantine and the Vikings in invading England'; the English won at Brunanburh.

wars.name: Norman invasion of Wales
wars.outcome: 'Initially (1067-1081)' without 'fervour and purpose'; a castle at Caerleon 'by 1086', ending Gwent; 'by 1094 most of Wales was under the control of William's son and heir'; by 1101 the Welsh 'had regained control of the greater part of their country'.

certainty.note: The shape is a residual between the Saxon, Welsh and Scottish rows and has no treaty or survey line in 800 years.
